blocks.heading: When ownership and control separate
blocks.text: Ownership is the right to hold the enterprise or an interest in it. Control concerns directing its decisions. In a small owner-managed enterprise the same person often provides finance and directs daily work. As a company grows, numerous shareholders may own shares while directors and professional managers make operational decisions. The board sets direction and oversees management; shareholders retain ownership rights such as voting under the ownership arrangements, but most do not run individual shifts. This is separation, or divorce, of ownership from control. It can bring specialist management and free owners from daily supervision. It can also create a conflict of interests: managers might favour expansion, status or their remuneration when owners prefer a higher return. Reporting, oversight and appropriate performance objectives can help align the interests, though they do not make every conflict disappear. Growth does not inevitably remove an owner from control; a founder with a controlling interest may retain strong influence. Explain who owns and who actually decides in the given situation.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Ombutu Packaging has many small shareholders. A professional manager chooses daily work schedules and proposes a larger head office. Shareholders want improved returns. Day-to-day control lies with management although ownership remains with shareholders. A larger office might benefit coordination, but it could also reflect managerial preferences. The board should assess its business benefit against cost and owners’ objectives instead of assuming all expansion serves shareholders.
